claim: The basal ganglia are known to bias movement selection according to value.
source: The basal ganglia are known to bias movement selection according to value, one form of internal goal.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Activity in the substantia nigra pars reticulata predictably differed preceding internally-specified and stimulus-guided movements.
source: We found that activity in the substantia nigra pars reticulata, a basal ganglia output, predictably differed preceding internally-specified and stimulus-guided movements.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Internally-specified movements may be facilitated relative to stimulus-guided movements by basal ganglia processing.
source: Incorporating these results into a simple model suggests that internally-specified movements may be facilitated relative to stimulus-guided movements by basal ganglia processing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on modeling of the experimental data.

claim: The basal ganglia contribute to movement selection by modulating inhibition on competing downstream motor structures.
source: The basal ganglia (BG) are known to be involved in motor control (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1989; Mink, 1996), contributing to movement selection by modulating inhibition on competing downstream motor structures (Basso and Wurtz, 2002; Di Chiara et al., 1979; Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Activity in several BG nuclei is modulated, prior to stimulus presentation, by reward expectation.
source: This 'value-biasing' hypothesis is supported by much evidence showing that activity in several BG nuclei is modulated, prior to stimulus presentation, by reward expectation (Bryden et al., 2011; Handel and Glimcher, 2000; Hikosaka et al., 2006; Kawagoe et al., 1998; Sato and Hikosaka, 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Movements toward high-value targets are disinhibited relative to movements toward low-value targets.
source: such that movements toward high-value targets are disinhibited relative to movements toward low-value targets (Hikosaka et al., 2006; Lauwereyns et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Movement selection may be guided by internal representations such as recent movements and their outcomes.
source: However, movement selection may also be guided by other internal representations, such as recent movements and their outcomes (Corrado et al., 2005; Fecteau and Munoz, 2003; Lau and Glimcher, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Parkinsonian patients exhibit more pronounced bradykinesia when initiating internally-specified than stimulus-guided movements.
source: Notably, it is has been proposed that Parkinsonian patients exhibit more pronounced bradykinesia when initiating internally-specified than stimulus-guided movements because the latter engage pathways outside of the BG (Glickstein and Stein, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The substantia nigra pars reticulata is an output nucleus of the BG critical for orienting movements.
source: We distinguished between these two possibilities by recording from neurons in the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), an output nucleus of the BG critical for orienting movements (Basso and Sommer, 2011; Handel and Glimcher, 1999; Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mice were able to infer unsignaled transitions between the SG and IS blocks and switch their response mode accordingly.
source: We found that mice were able to infer (unsignaled) transitions between the SG and IS blocks and switch their response mode accordingly: during SG blocks, mice were equally likely to choose the left and right port (Figure 1C, gray boxes) reflecting a dependence on the odor mixture (Figure 1D), while during IS blocks, mice reliably returned to the same (rewarded) port in each trial (Figure 1C, white boxes).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Reaction time was shorter in IS trials than in easy SG trials.
source: Indeed, across the population of sessions, we found that reaction time – defined as the time from the go cue to reward port entry – was shorter in IS trials than in the 'easy' SG trials in the same session [Figure 1F; we used only easy SG trials (mixture ratios of 95/5, 80/20, 20/80, and 5/95) to control for a potential dependence of reaction time on difficulty; population of sessions: p = 1.7 × 10−11, paired t-test; individual sessions: IS shorter than SG in 46/108, SG shorter than IS in 3/108, p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; ipsiversive and contraversive trials compared separately].
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 216 out of 296 neurons displayed a significant direction preference during the delay epoch.
source: We found that 216/296 neurons displayed a significant direction preference (p<0.05) during the delay epoch, with about as many preferring ipsiversive (94/216) as contraversive (122/216) movements (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 188 out of 296 neurons exhibited an increase in activity during the delay epoch relative to baseline.
source: We found that 188/296 neurons exhibited an increase in activity during this epoch, 91/296 exhibited a decrease, and 17/296 exhibited no change (Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neural recording data shown in Table 1.

claim: SNr activity exhibits both movement-related increases and decreases.
source: Since SNr activity has been shown to exhibit both movement-related increases and decreases (Bryden et al., 2011; Gulley et al., 2002, 1999; Handel and Glimcher, 1999; Sato and Hikosaka, 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neurons tended to show a larger difference in firing rate between ipsiversive and contraversive movements in IS than in SG trials.
source: Across our population, neurons tended to show a larger difference in firing rate preceding ipsiversive and contraversive movements in IS than in SG trials [Figure 3D; ipsiversive-preferring neurons: p = 2.2 × 10−10, paired t-test; contraversive-preferring neurons: p = 4.0 × 10−4, paired t-test].
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Approximately half of direction-selective neurons were modulated by trial type for trials in the preferred direction.
source: For trials in the preferred direction, we found that the activity of approximately half of the direction-selective neurons was modulated by trial type (101/216; p<0.05, unpaired t-test), with more neurons exhibiting higher activity in IS trials than SG trials (84/101 vs. 17/101; p = 2.6 × 10−11, X2 test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data.

claim: For trials in the antipreferred direction, more neurons exhibited higher activity in SG trials than IS trials.
source: Conversely, for trials in the antipreferred direction, we again found that the activity of approximately half of the direction-selective neurons was modulated by trial type (109/216; p<0.05, unpaired t-test; 158/216 direction-selective neurons were modulated by trial type in at least one direction), but that more neurons exhibited higher activity in SG trials than IS trials (76/109 vs. 33/109; p = 3.8 × 10−5, X2 test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data.

claim: 77 out of 158 neurons exhibited a significant correlation between firing rate and the number of consecutive correct trials.
source: Overall, 77/158 neurons exhibited a significant correlation (p<0.05) between firing rate and the number of consecutive correct trials for either direction [Figure 4B,C; 35/77 for trials in the preferred direction (red circles), 29/77 for trials in the antipreferred direction (blue circles), and 13/77 for trials in both directions (purple circles)]
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: More neurons showed positive correlations for trials in the preferred direction and negative correlations for trials in the antipreferred direction.
source: with more positive correlations for trials in the preferred direction (p = 2.4 × 10−6, X2 test) and negative correlations for trials in the antipreferred direction (p = 5.9 × 10−6, X2 test), as we would expect given the pattern of results shown in Figure 3D.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data.

claim: Easy SG trials resulted in a larger fraction of correct choices than difficult SG trials.
source: Were this the case, we would expect to observe a difference in activity between those SG trials requiring an easy discrimination (mixture ratios of 95/5, 80/20, 20/80, and 5/95) and those SG trials requiring a 'difficult' discrimination (mixture ratios of 60/40, 50/50, and 40/60), since easy trials resulted in a larger fraction of correct choices (p = 3.4 × 10–27, paired t-test; see Figure 1D), corresponding to a higher likelihood of reward.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The activity of some individual neurons depended on difficulty or an associated variable.
source: We found that the activity of some individual neurons depended on difficulty (or an associated variable) (ipsiversive direction: 39/216 neurons; contraversive direction: 31/216 neurons, p<0.05, 1-way ANOVA across mixture ratios, Figure 5A,B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: There was little overlap between difficulty-dependent neurons and trial-type-dependent neurons.
source: However, there was little overlap (purple circles) between this small population of difficulty-dependent neurons (blue circles) and those neurons that we classified as trial-type-dependent [ipsiversive direction: 21/109 trial-type-dependent, and 18/107 non-trial-type-dependent, neurons exhibited difficulty dependence (these ratios did not differ: p = 0.32, X2 test); contraversive direction: 16/101 trial-type-dependent, and 15/115 non-trial-type-dependent, neurons exhibited difficulty dependence (these ratios did not differ: p = 0.56, X2 test); p<0.05, 1-way ANOVA across mixture ratios].
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data.

claim: Differences in decision difficulty, uncertainty, and the value associated with the direction of movement do not account for trial-type dependence.
source: These results suggest that differences in decision difficulty, uncertainty, and the value associated with the direction of movement do not account for trial-type dependence or the differences in activity between SG and IS trials shown in Figure 3D.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of neural recording data.

claim: The vast majority of neurons (281/296) were influenced by at least one of the factors: previous choice, current choice, trial type, or reaction time.
source: Across our population of neurons, the vast majority were influenced by at least one of these factors (281/296, p<0.05), and we found neurons with firing rates influenced by all possible combinations of factors (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of neural recording data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The activity of many SNr neurons was modulated by current choice (167/296) during the delay epoch.
source: Consistent with the results shown in Figure 3C and D, respectively, this analysis confirms that, as the mouse is selecting its direction of movement, the activity of many SNr neurons was modulated by current choice (167/296) and trial type (142/296).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of neural recording data.

claim: The activity of many SNr neurons was modulated by trial type (142/296) during the delay epoch.
source: Consistent with the results shown in Figure 3C and D, respectively, this analysis confirms that, as the mouse is selecting its direction of movement, the activity of many SNr neurons was modulated by current choice (167/296) and trial type (142/296).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of neural recording data.

claim: The activity of many neurons depended on reaction time (111/296).
source: We also found that the activity of many neurons depended on reaction time (111/296).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of neural recording data.

claim: The largest fraction of neurons exhibited activity modulated by previous choice (188/296).
source: Surprisingly, the largest fraction of neurons exhibited activity modulated by previous choice (188/296).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of neural recording data.

claim: Previous choice is critical for determining which direction is associated with reward in an IS block.
source: This is particularly interesting because this variable is critical for determining, in an IS block, which direction is associated with reward.
evidence: This is an inference based on the task design and the role of previous choice in IS blocks.

claim: Before the odor is delivered, the firing rates of about half of the neurons are influenced by the previous choice.
source: Before the odor is delivered, the firing rates of about half of the neurons are influenced by the previous choice.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of neural recording data across time windows shown in Figure 6C.

claim: As the odor is sampled, the influence of the previous choice decreases and the influence of the current choice increases.
source: However, as the odor is sampled, the influence of the previous choice decreases and the influence of the current choice increases, with about two thirds of neurons exhibiting a significant weight for the current choice by the time the movement is initiated.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of neural recording data across time windows shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Trial type modulates the activity of about one third of neurons throughout the trial.
source: Interestingly, trial type modulates the activity of about one third of neurons throughout the trial.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of neural recording data across time windows shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SNr activity preceding orienting movements depends on whether the direction of movement was indicated by a stimulus or was specified by internal variables.
source: We have shown that SNr activity preceding orienting movements depends on whether the direction of movement was indicated by a stimulus or was specified by internal variables (Figures 3, 4).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The dependence on trial type could not be accounted for by differences in the estimated value of each movement direction between the trial types.
source: However, the dependence on trial type could not be accounted for by differences in the estimated value of each movement direction – or an associated variable, such as difficulty or uncertainty in selecting the movement – between the trial types (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In some neurons, the dependence on trial type could be explained, in part, by the choice on the previous trial.
source: In some neurons this dependence could be explained, in part, by the choice on the previous trial (Figure 6A), which is informative of the rewarded direction in IS blocks.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Over the course of the trial, the influence on SNr activity of the previous choice decreased and that of the current choice increased, while the influence of trial type remained relatively constant.
source: Over the course of the trial, while the influence on SNr activity of the previous choice decreased and that of the current choice increased, as might be expected given the demands of the task, the influence of trial type remained relatively constant (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis across time windows shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The SNr is differentially engaged by stimulus-guided and internally-specified movements.
source: These results suggest that the SNr is differentially engaged by stimulus-guided and internally-specified movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Movement-related SNr activity was higher for memory-guided than visually-guided saccades in primates.
source: Previous studies in primates have shown that movement-related SNr activity was higher for memory-guided than visually-guided saccades (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983a)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: SNr stimulation had a larger effect on memory- than visually-guided saccades in primates.
source: and that SNr stimulation had a larger effect on memory- than visually-guided saccades (Basso and Liu, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The results generalize across species and movement types (saccades and full-body orienting).
source: Movements selected based on a remembered stimulus can be thought of as internally specified, and in this sense our results (Figure 3D) are consistent with these findings and demonstrate that they generalize across species and movement types (saccades and full-body orienting).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the current results with prior research.

claim: In IS trials, direction preference sometimes emerged even before stimulus delivery.
source: However, the rewarded direction in both memory- and visually-guided trials was indicated by the stimulus, which was not the case in our IS trials, in which we sometimes observed that direction preference emerged even before stimulus delivery (see example in Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by observation of neural recording data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The difference between direction preference in IS and SG trials during the delay epoch was correlated with the difference between preference in IS and SG trials during the epoch from odor port entry to odor valve open.
source: Further, the difference between direction preference in IS and SG trials during the delay epoch was correlated with the difference between preference in IS and SG trials during the epoch from odor port entry to odor valve open (r = 0.47, p = 4.8 × 10−18).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neural recording data.

claim: In IS trials, the direction of movement was initially selected independent of the stimulus.
source: These results demonstrate that, in IS trials, the direction of movement was initially selected independent of the stimulus, which contributes to the difference in activity during the delay epoch that we observe between SG and IS trials.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis of neural recording data.

claim: All groups of neurons (increasing and decreasing, preferring ipsiversive and contraversive movement) exhibited a difference in activity between stimulus-guided and internally-specified movements.
source: In addition, while Hikosaka and Wurtz (1983a) examined only neurons that exhibited a decrease in activity around the time of contraversive saccades, we examined increasing and decreasing neurons that prefer both ipsiversive and contraversive movement (Gulley et al., 2002, 1999; Handel and Glimcher, 2000; Sato and Hikosaka, 2002) and found that all of these groups exhibited a difference in activity between stimulus-guided and internally-specified movements.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neural recording data across different neuron types.

claim: Patients with Parkinson's disease and other BG pathologies exhibit greater deficits in the initiation of internally-specified than visually-guided movements.
source: Interestingly, patients with Parkinson's disease and other BG pathologies have been reported to exhibit greater deficits in the initiation of internally-specified than visually-guided movements (Forssberg et al., 1984; Laplane et al., 1984; Azulay et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior clinical research.

claim: Visual cues may engage intact sensorimotor pathways outside of the BG, such as the cerebellum.
source: While the neural basis for this phenomenon is not well understood and remains an active area of study (Distler et al., 2016), it has been suggested that visual cues engage (intact) sensorimotor pathways outside of the BG, such as the cerebellum (Glickstein and Stein, 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Differential processing of internally-specified and visually-guided movements within the BG themselves may contribute to the clinical observation of greater deficits in Parkinsonian patients for internally-specified movements.
source: Our results suggest that differential processing of internally-specified and visually-guided movements within the BG themselves may also contribute to this clinical observation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data and prior clinical observations.

claim: Movement-related SNr activity is modulated by the relative value associated with a movement.
source: As noted above, other studies have found that movement-related SNr activity is modulated by the relative value associated with a movement (Bryden et al., 2011; Sato and Hikosaka, 2002), including whether the movement will be rewarded at all (Handel and Glimcher, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Value dependence in SNr activity likely arises from dopaminergic input to the BG that conveys reward-related information.
source: This value dependence likely arises from dopaminergic input to the BG that is thought to convey reward-related information (Schultz et al., 1997)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A model in which reward expectation modulates striatal inputs to the SNr to bias downstream superior colliculus activity can account for how the most valuable movement is facilitated.
source: and has been accounted for by a model in which, prior to stimulus presentation, reward expectation modulates striatal inputs to the SNr in order to bias downstream superior colliculus (SC) activity such that the most valuable movement is facilitated (Hikosaka et al., 2006; Wolf et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: A similar model can explain how internally-specified movements, more generally, are facilitated.
source: We propose that a similar model can also explain how internally-specified movements, more generally, are facilitated (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on extending a prior model to the current data, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Left and right SNr neurons would exhibit a larger difference in activity in IS trials than in SG trials for an upcoming rightward movement.
source: To illustrate this idea, consider how, given the data presented here, the relative activity between ipsiversive-preferring left and right SNr neurons would relate to an upcoming rightward movement (we consider relative, rather than absolute, activity since this is most directly relevant to the decision – move left vs. move right – required by our task). Left and right SNr neurons would exhibit a larger difference in activity in IS trials than in SG trials (Figure 3D, left).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ipsiversive-preferring SNr neurons primarily project to the ipsilateral SC.
source: If ipsiversive-preferring SNr neurons primarily project to the ipsilateral SC (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983b)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research and is presented as a conditional assumption.

claim: A downstream left SC neuron will receive less inhibition from the left SNr when the movement is internally specified, thereby facilitating rightward movements that are internally specified.
source: then a downstream left SC neuron, the activity of which promotes rightward movement (Felsen and Mainen, 2012; Horwitz and Newsome, 2001; Stubblefield et al., 2013) will receive less inhibition from the left SNr when the movement is internally specified, thereby facilitating rightward movements that are internally specified (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and data, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Contraversive-preferring SNr neurons comprise the 'crossed' projection to the contralateral SC.
source: If contraversive-preferring SNr neurons comprise the 'crossed' projection to the contralateral SC (Jiang et al., 2003)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research and is presented as a conditional assumption.

claim: A downstream right SC neuron would receive more inhibition from the left SNr when the movement is internally specified, again facilitating the rightward movement.
source: then a downstream right SC neuron would receive more inhibition from the left SNr when the movement is internally specified, again facilitating the rightward movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and data.

claim: Slightly more SNr neurons prefer contraversive than ipsiversive movement.
source: However, we observed that slightly more SNr neurons prefer contraversive than ipsiversive movement (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Many fewer SNr neurons project to the contralateral than ipsilateral SC, particularly in rodents.
source: but many fewer SNr neurons project to the contralateral than ipsilateral SC, particularly in rodents (Beckstead et al., 1981; Deniau et al., 1977; Gerfen et al., 1982; Jayaraman et al., 1977)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior anatomical research.

claim: Contraversive-preferring SNr neurons may preferentially project to non-tectal targets.
source: and contraversive-preferring SNr neurons may preferentially project to non-tectal targets.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on anatomical considerations.

claim: SNr activity may be consistent with the facilitation of internally-specified contraversive movements.
source: Thus, SNr activity may be consistent with the facilitation of internally-specified contraversive movements.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the model and anatomical considerations.

claim: The results extend the model underlying the value-biasing view of BG function by suggesting that the influence of the SNr on downstream motor regions is modulated by internal representations in addition to value.
source: Our results therefore extend the model underlying the value-biasing view of BG function (Hikosaka et al., 2006) by suggesting that the influence of the SNr on downstream motor regions is modulated by internal representations in addition to value.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and prior models.

claim: Internal representations of priors play a critical role in guiding motor output.
source: We suggest that this dependence may reflect a facilitation for internally-specified movements, consistent with the view that, although movements are often made in response to sensory stimuli, internal representations of priors play a critical role in guiding motor output (Wolpert and Landy, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The results are sufficiently consistent with results in primate SNr that they can inform the interpretation of previous studies.
source: Our results are sufficiently consistent with results in primate SNr (Handel and Glimcher, 2000, 1999; Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983a; Liu and Basso, 2008; Sato and Hikosaka, 2002) that they can inform the interpretation of previous studies (e.g., our proposed extensions of the model explaining the value-biasing role of the BG described above), while also offering novel insight into BG function.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the current results with prior research.

claim: 296 well-isolated left SNr neurons were recorded from four mice performing the task.
source: We recorded from 296 well-isolated left SNr neurons (see Materials and methods; Figure 2) in four mice performing the task (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: Male adult C57BL/6J mice aged 7–14 months at the start of experiments were used.
source: We used male adult C57BL/6J mice (n = 4, determined by estimating the number of neurons required for our analyses and by the number of neurons recorded per mouse in initial experiments; aged 7–14 months at the start of experiments; Jackson Labs)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Mice were housed in a vivarium with a 12-hr light/dark cycle with lights on at 5:00 am.
source: housed in a vivarium with a 12-hr light/dark cycle with lights on at 5:00 am.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: Access to water was restricted to the behavioral session to motivate performance.
source: Access to water was restricted to the behavioral session to motivate performance; however, if mice did not obtain ~1 ml of water during the behavioral session, additional water was provided for ~2–5 min following the behavioral session (Smear et al., 2011; Thompson and Felsen, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: All mice were weighed daily and received sufficient water during behavioral sessions to maintain >85% of pre-water restriction weight.
source: All mice were weighed daily and received sufficient water during behavioral sessions to maintain >85% of pre-water restriction weight.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Odors were comprised of binary mixtures of (+)-carvone and (-)-carvone, commonly perceived as caraway and spearmint, respectively.
source: Odors were comprised of binary mixtures of (+)-carvone and (-)-carvone, commonly perceived as caraway and spearmint, respectively; an enantiomeric odor pair was selected to control for differences in molecular structure of odorant stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Mice learned to perform SG trials within approximately 48 sessions.
source: Mice learned to perform SG trials within ~48 sessions (1 session/day); detailed training stages are described in Stubblefield et al. (2013).
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral training.

claim: Mice required an additional approximately 5 sessions to learn to perform interleaved blocks of SG and IS trials.
source: Mice required an additional ~5 sessions to learn to perform interleaved blocks of SG and IS trials.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral training.

claim: During each of the 54 recording sessions, mice performed 321.81 ± 89.49 (mean ± SD) trials.
source: During each of the 54 recording sessions, mice performed 321.81 ± 89.49 (mean ± SD) trials.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral performance during recording sessions.

claim: Tetrodes were moved approximately 62.5 μm between sessions.
source: One full rotation moved the tetrode ~250 μm and tetrodes were moved ~62.5 μm between sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the recording procedure.

claim: Clusters with an L-ratio of less than 0.70 and isolation distance greater than 6.5 were deemed single units.
source: Clusters with an L-ratio of less than 0.70 and isolation distance greater than 6.5 were deemed single units, which resulted in the exclusion of 12% of the identified clusters.
evidence: This is a description of the spike sorting criteria.

claim: 12% of the identified clusters were excluded based on quality metrics.
source: Clusters with an L-ratio of less than 0.70 and isolation distance greater than 6.5 were deemed single units, which resulted in the exclusion of 12% of the identified clusters.
evidence: This is a description of the data exclusion criteria.
